title: The minefield called footpath
author: Vijaya Bharat
content_html:
My husband returned from his morning walk with a bruised knee. He had stumbled on a footpath. As he lay spreadeagled and shaken, two women looked at him from the corner of their eyes and walked past. More than the injury, he felt bad that the women had probably assumed that he had a drink too many and left him to his plight. Soon a few men rushed in and helped him to get up and offered to accompany him home.

He told me that the bruise on his knee was superficial but the hurt on his ego was deep: the episode was embarrassing and frightening. I didn’t want to rub salt on the wound by accusing him of walking carelessly and advise him to be mindful and to watch his steps. Glad that I didn’t lecture, because the very next day, I too fell on another footpath. The front part of my shoe got caught in a crevice and I fell face down. Though there was no bodily injury, I was concerned about my spectacles. One of the photochromatic progressive lenses fell from its frame. I too was fortunate not to sustain any injury and got up with embarrassment as people collected offering help.

Stunning blow

At 70-plus, my husband and I travel extensively and believe that physical fitness and mental alertness will make us enjoy the autumn of our lives. We became aware that such falls can break a bone or two, confine us to bed for long periods and lead to complications with collateral damage to other body systems, affecting recovery. Under such unfortunate circumstances, age will not be just a number but an important factor deciding recovery or otherwise.

When I advise my patients to walk and be active, many of them complain that there is no safe place to walk. Footpaths almost everywhere are dug, badly repaired, and dug again. While many modern houses are kept clean on the inside, construction debris and waste materials are thrown on the no-man’s land — the footpath.

In most places, the paver blocks are loose or broken and pathways resemble a corrugated cardboard with random dips and mounds in addition to heaps of dog poop and cow dung. In some otherwise good footpaths, overhanging plants, some thorny, make the pedestrians stoop or step on to the road. Moreover, it is not at all uncommon for hawkers to display their products and shops to extend into the footpath and for two-wheelers to be parked.

Considering all these deterrents, I started to walk on roads adjacent to the footpath. On a morning walk, a motorcyclist leaned sideways and tried to grab a gold chain from my neck. He didn’t succeed and I decided to avoid such threats by removing jewellery and keeping my mobile phone in the pocket of my track pants. One of my patients, also walking, advised me to face the incoming traffic to avoid getting hit from behind. I soon realised that any vehicle could come from any direction anytime. With no control on that factor, I carry a hiking stick to ward off stray dogs.

Despite all such threats, I continue to walk and wholeheartedly welcome the Supreme Court declaration that the right to walk safely on well-maintained footpaths is a Fundamental Right in the Constitution. On a recent trip to Taipei, Taiwan we were happy to experience what safe walking can feel like. My husband and I were excited and impressed with the green-coloured even footpaths with a painting of a man holding a child, even in small lanes. There were separate tracks for cycles and everywhere motor vehicles were parked on only one side of the lane, well within the marked areas. Traffic signals were working and rules were followed even when the traffic was light. At zebra crossings, there were clear displays indicating that pedestrians have the right of way.

All the above-mentioned events happened within a span of one month.

On our return flight, we hoped that the civil authorities will make the footpaths safe and the public will comply with a strong civic sense. The onus is on everyone.

title: Beyond Gen Z lingo
author: Sindhu  Sarma
content_html:
On one recent trip, I snapped at my eight-year-old son. What he said to my husband and me a few minutes later took us completely by surprise. And it has been coming back to me often ever since.

I had just had an argument with a staff member at a food outlet. We were getting back into the car, but my son was a little slow getting in. He was about to ask me a question when I snapped, “Why don’t you ever listen to what I tell you to do?” My husband, trying to help, added curtly, “Chittu, listen to Amma.”

About five minutes into the drive, my son, holding back tears, quietly asked, “You and Amma said I didn’t listen to what you were saying. What did I not listen to?”

We were both taken aback. The truth was he had not done anything wrong. It was just my own displaced frustration from my conversation with the staff member.

What was remarkable and even embarrassing was the clarity of his question. In those few minutes, he must have replayed the interaction in his mind and arrived at that simple, logical question. He wasn’t being argumentative or disrespectful. And he was right — we did not have an answer.

Lately, this question comes back to me whenever I watch young people question decisions they believe are unfair. It makes me wonder whether what we are witnessing is a profound shift in how the next generation relates to authority. While we discuss their slang, their memes, and their digital habits, perhaps language is the least interesting thing about this generation. The real shift here is not linguistic; it is about values.

Gen Z has grown up with greater access to information than any generation before them. Many more than in the previous generations have been raised by parents who, less consumed by fight for survival, were able to encourage self-expression and confidence. The language they grew up with is one of rights, dignity, authenticity, mental health, inclusion, and accountability.

Given this background, it is but natural that they are going to be less quietly deferential to authority and institutions as the millennials and the generation before them. They recognise trauma patterns at home. They are going to call out toxic workspaces and unreasonable bosses. The ideals of accountability and transparency, once discussed in aspirational terms in public administration textbooks, have moved to everyday expectations citizens have of their civic institutions.

This has implications for our public service delivery mechanisms.

Preparing institutions

If institutions are to reflect the values of the next generation, the place to begin is with the everyday experience of citizens.

A birth certificate should be issued for the 25 rupees it is meant to cost. Every child should have access to a nearby municipal park to play in the evenings. Becoming a homeowner should not require navigating a maze of middlemen to secure building permission, electricity or water connections. Buying an apartment should come with the assurance that it has been built to code. A visit to a police station or government office should not be accompanied by apprehension or the need to know someone who knows someone. A visit to a government hospital should not leave patients wondering whether the doctor will show up. Pursuing a business idea, big or small, should not mean navigating a myriad of palms to grease. A land title should actually mean something — not merely until someone chooses to encroach upon it.

A choreography

Where procedures remain dependent on delay, discretion, and middlemen, graft is not chaos. It is choreography. A choreography that previous generations often resigned themselves to, but one that the next generation is far more likely to question.

There are many proposals for deeper institutional reform. But we can begin with something simpler, and perhaps more transformative: placing citizens at the centre of public service delivery.

Beyond fixing systems, we need a shift in mindset so that an ordinary citizen can secure what is already theirs — not as a favour, but as a matter of right.

My son’s question still echoes in my mind. “What did I not listen to?” To me, it was a question that exposed the gap between authority and fairness.

We are witnessing a generational shift in how citizens relate to authority.

The real challenge with Gen Z isn’t learning their language — it’s adapting to what they value. Accountability and transparency are no longer aspirations (they are expectations). Public service must now be designed for citizens who will no longer accept opacity, delay, discretion or graft as inevitable.

(Views are personal)

title: Gnawing memories
author: Raj  Laxmi Verma
content_html:
Seven months after my cousin’s death, I still see him on my phone.

Sometimes Google Photos surprises me with an old picture. Sometimes I come across one of his social media posts while scrolling. For a brief moment, it feels as though he has returned. Then reality catches up. The photograph remains, but he does not. What appears on the screen is not a person, only a memory waiting to be rediscovered.

Experiences like this were rare for previous generations. When someone died, their photographs stayed inside albums and their letters remained tucked away in drawers. Unless family members deliberately searched for them, those memories often stayed out of sight. Today, however, the dead continue to appear in our digital lives long after they are gone.

For most of human history, people were said to die twice. The first death was physical. The second came much later, when memories faded and stories stopped being told. Eventually, even those who were deeply loved disappeared from everyday conversation. Their names survived in family records, old photographs, and the minds of a few remaining relatives.

The second death was not sudden. It arrived slowly, often across generations. In this sense, forgetting was once an unavoidable part of being human.

Today, that second death appears to have been postponed.

The Internet has transformed the way we remember. Ordinary people now leave behind thousands of photographs, messages, emails, videos, and social media posts. Long after someone has died, we can still see their face, hear their voice, and read their thoughts. Future generations may know their grandparents and great-grandparents in ways that were impossible only a few decades ago.

Digital technology has created something unique in human history. Never before have so many people left such detailed records of their everyday lives. A birthday photograph, a casual text message or a short video clip can survive indefinitely, stored on servers scattered across the world. The result is a vast archive of ordinary human existence.

In many ways, this is a gift. A photograph can revive a forgotten smile. A video can preserve a laugh that might otherwise have disappeared with time. A simple message can bring back an ordinary conversation that suddenly becomes precious after someone is gone.

Yet there is another side to this gift.

We can preserve memories better than ever before, but losing someone still hurts just as much. Sometimes technology even makes grief more complicated. Just when life begins to settle into a new normal, an old photograph appears unexpectedly. A social media platform reminds us of a post from years ago. The past returns without invitation.

A photograph can remind us of someone, but it cannot replace a conversation. A saved message cannot answer a new question. A video can replay a laugh, but it cannot create a new memory. The photographs matter because the person mattered. The files matter because the relationship mattered.

A footprint on a beach proves that someone once walked there. But the footprint is not the person. It is only a trace of a presence that has already moved on.

Digital memories are much the same. They remind us that someone was here, that they laughed, loved and shared a part of their journey with us. The Internet may have delayed the second death, the fading of memory, but it cannot preserve the one thing we miss most. It cannot preserve a person’s presence.

title: The high of anonymity
author: S. Radha Prathi
content_html:
For the longest time, we have been witnessing people who migrate to other countries in search of greener pastures. Over a period of time, they settle down in an alien land for good.

A similar scenario is being replayed in Bengaluru. Lots and lots of young people from all walks of life have been surging into the city lock, stock and barrel.

Recently, I had the opportunity to interact with a wide spectrum of staff members who work for a construction company. They were a mix of the educated and no so educated, men and women, urban and rural, speaking different languages, belonging to diverse age groups and backgrounds. Almost all of them had come kit and caboodle from different parts of the northern and neighbouring States. They were gushing praise for the garden city.

The newcomers have taken to it, like a duck takes to water. Signs of balding greenery, rising concrete buildings, mindless drilling of borewells, maddening crowds, and insane traffic seems invisible to some of these guest workers. They feel that the jam-packed roads and rationed water are inconsequential in the face of what the Silicon Valley offers them. Salubrious weather, verdant lung spaces, and the urban aura appeal to them.

They have identified their favourite comfort zones to blend into the fabric of their second home. Besides, they have formed their own groups and associations to keep in touch with their regional and cultural roots. Their taste buds relish the local cuisine and they have also identified oases in the metropolis which caters for their niche traditional menu as mother makes it. The local people accommodate them, though they are not familiar with the vernacular. Technology has ensured that they are in touch with their loved ones in real time. All the same, the newly endeared city dares them with its dearness. Some of them in the lower rungs of the economic ladder do get to bear the brunt of it from time to time.

Yet, interestingly, not one of them wanted to return to their native places. It was certainly not a lack of sentimental or nostalgic values about their backyard. All of them were keen on visiting their kith and kin as and when possible. It was then I realised, that new prospects and material benefits could not be the only reasons for their relocation.

On scratching the surface, to check what made them synergise without reluctance, the responses though articulated variously boiled down to one factor. In Bengaluru, they could lead their lives incognito, without being judged by society, and explore their potential without being judged. They had tasted personal liberty which was hitherto unknown in the small towns and villages they hailed from. Their sense of universal belonging stemmed from this sense of freedom which made their second home their home.

This unexpected but sound logic for their conscious choice reflected the essence of the famous line of the Tamil Sangam poet Kaniyan Poongunranar. He summed up their collective emotions a few millennia ago in his famous line Yaadhum oore yaavarum keleer, which translates as “All towns are mine and all people are mine”.

title: Rain-soaked memories
author: K.S.S. Pillai
content_html:
The heavy rain had stopped after days of destruction, killing some and wounding many. With clear skies, it appeared that the summer had come back. I was not sure whether it was the effect of El Niño, playing havoc with the climate in many parts of the world, as reported in the media.

While going to sleep, I had switched on the air-conditioner in my bedroom, keeping the temperature cool enough to sleep, and kept the ceiling fans rotating at maximum speed. The windows had been shut, preventing the airflow.

Electricity supply frequently disappears in the city where I reside. As often happens, the supply stopped at the dead of night, and the ceiling fan and air-conditioner stopped working. Soon I woke up, sweating profusely.

There was no telling when the supply would be restored, as it usually took much time even during the daytime.

That took me back to my childhood in my village. Our house, like most others in the village, was thatched with woven coconut leaves, seasoned in the flowing waters of the nearby river. Electricity was a new entrant, and the public roads had burning bulbs on wooden poles at night. Only the rich had their tiled houses electrified. They had bulbs in all rooms, in place of different types of kerosene lamps. Mine was one of the houses without an electricity connection.

My siblings and I slept on mats made of the seasoned plant leaves spread on the floor, which was periodically plastered with mud and cow dung. Air passed through the coconut leaves on the roof, making the rooms cool with all their open windows.

The thatch was renewed every year with the participation of all able-bodied neighbours. It was like a festival. The women gathered, preparing meals for all on makeshift hearths, and enjoyed exchanging gossip.

As the houses used hearths to cook food, the old coconut leaves that burned brightly, emitting little smoke, were welcomed by the women of the house. They were stored nearby, considering that the rainwater did not dampen them.

Every house had some trees like mango and cashew in its compound. Usually, their branches swayed in the gentle breeze during the day, the people sitting in their shadows not much affected by the high temperature. The trees were pruned every year, and their dry branches and leaves were used in the hearths. The children were experts at hanging swings from the branches, and they spent afternoons swinging and eating the fruits of those trees.

Most men had their upper bodies bare, with a white towel called “thorthu” tied on their heads to wipe away sweat. Everybody bathed in the nearby Pampa river in the morning and evening. Some people visited the local temple, binding dripping towels around their lower bodies and smearing their foreheads with the sandalwood paste handed out by the priest.

I think people were better placed to face the change in the weather then.

That took me back to my childhood in my village. Our house, like most others in the village, was thatched with woven coconut leaves, seasoned in the flowing waters of the nearby river. Electricity was a new entrant, and the public roads had burning bulbs on wooden poles at night. Only the rich had their tiled houses electrified. They had bulbs in all rooms, in place of different types of kerosene lamps. Mine was one of the houses without an electricity connection.
My siblings and I slept on mats made of the seasoned plant leaves spread on the floor, which was periodically plastered with mud and cow dung. Air passed through the coconut leaves on the roof, making the rooms cool with all their open windows.
The thatch was renewed every year with the participation of all able-bodied neighbours. It was like a festival. The women gathered, preparing meals for all on makeshift hearths, and enjoyed exchanging gossip.
As the houses used hearths to cook food, the old coconut leaves that burned brightly, emitting little smoke, were welcomed by the women of the house. They were stored nearby, considering that the rainwater did not dampen them.
Every house had some trees like mango and cashew in its compound. Usually, their branches swayed in the gentle breeze during the day, the people sitting in their shadows not much affected by the high temperature. The trees were pruned every year, and their dry branches and leaves were used in the hearths. The children were experts at hanging swings from the branches, and they spent afternoons swinging and eating the fruits of those trees.
Most men had their upper bodies bare, with a white towel called “thorthu” tied on their heads to wipe away sweat. Everybody bathed in the nearby Pampa river in the morning and evening. Some people visited the local temple, binding dripping towels around their lower bodies and smearing their foreheads with the sandalwood paste handed out by the priest.
I think people were better placed to face the change in the weather then.

title: Bullying is not a rite of passage
author: Aufaq  Zargar
content_html:
There are some images that we cannot shake off. Not because they are harrowing, but because they show something far more disturbing, the quiet crumbling of humanity in places where it should be strongest. A girl stands inside her classroom — hands crossed, head bowed, eyes begging for attention, searching for reassurance. Nearby other children are laughing. There is a teacher close by. Moments later the child runs out. She does not come back.

It is the story of the death of a nine-year-old Class 4 student in Jaipur on November 1, 2025 that sparked a national debate about bullying and institutional responsibility. For weeks, the tragedy remained another painful headline. Then, eight months on, CCTV footage released by her grieving parents sent shockwaves across the nation. The family affirms the video is not only about a child being bullied but also about a child trying desperately to be heard. While investigations must establish the facts, one thing is beyond dispute: every frightened child deserves to be heard before despair becomes irreversible.

Children do not always have the words to express emotional pain. Instead, they speak in silence. As a way of shaking hands. Eyes down. Through tears. The family says she repeatedly went to her teacher, while other students allegedly taunted and humiliated her.

Of all that has been unveiled since that November afternoon, one detail has broken the hearts of parents. The child was scared of heights. If a child is afraid of heights, she will not be tempted to go near the edge of a four-storey building. Fear of heights is instinctive. Another fear must be greater for that instinct to be overpowered.

What passed through her mind in those last moments we may never know. Only she knew the weight she bore. But her mother’s words force us to consider a painful possibility: whatever happened to her inside that classroom may have felt, in that moment, more terrifying than the height she feared. That thought alone should keep every educator up. Her family asserts that the CCTV footage raises questions about whether her distress was dealt with immediately. Now those allegations are subject to greater public and institutional scrutiny. Whatever the result of the investigations, one thing cannot be disputed. If a scared child calls for help, adults must respond — not after the next lesson, not after the next meet. Right away.

Bullying is not a rite of passage. For generations now, adults have been comforting themselves with dangerous myths. “They’re only children.” “It will make them stronger.” “We all went through it.” Such words have condoned many acts of cruelty. Bullying isn’t just harmless fun. It is repeatedly humiliating to diminish another human being. Sometimes it hurts. More often it leaves invisible wounds that quietly settle into a child’s confidence, self-worth and sense of belonging.

A daily repeated nickname. The laughter that comes when one child talks. Being deliberately left out. The face of mockery. The whisper that the rest of the world hears. Each of these acts in itself does not seem to be catastrophic. They can convince a child, together, that school no longer becomes a place of learning, but a place of survival.

An experienced teacher knows that children will not keep coming to a teacher for help unless something is terribly wrong. A loud voice can be ignored. A complaint can be taken the wrong way. But repeated distress is never normal. It is a sign. And signals must be responded to. Teaching has never been just in textbooks. Decades later, a student may forget every equation and every date — but they will never forget the teacher who made them feel they belonged. Children rarely remember all chapters. They always remember how they were treated by teachers. Academic excellence loses its meaning if emotional safety is absent.

It would be comforting to believe this tragedy belongs to one institution. But it doesn’t. There are children in every city who hate Monday mornings. Every school has students who practise excuses to skip class. There is always one — the child who has stopped raising her hand, stopped speaking, stopped hoping, wondering if anyone would notice if they simply disappeared. Bullying takes many forms today. Sometimes it happens in the hallways. Sometimes in WhatsApp groups. Sometimes via social media. Sometimes in whispers teachers never hear. Sometimes in laughter all take for fun. The place is changing. The damage wasn’t.

When success outweighs safety

Today’s education system is about rankings, board results, university placements, smart classrooms, robotics labs and international collaborations. These achievements count. But they are hollow if a child doesn’t feel safe sitting at a desk. Parents don’t often ask what the school’s best exam results are before asking a much easier question. “Will my child be safe here?” That question merits more than the soothing words printed in a prospectus. It requires proof. Active anti-bullying committees. School counsellors on site. Teachers trained to recognise emotional distress. Systems that protect vulnerable children before tragedy strikes.

Safety is not an after-school activity. It is the first responsibility of education. Listen Before It Is Too Late. Children seldom tell you they are sinking emotionally. They whisper instead. Parents and teachers must learn to listen to what children cannot yet say. The dinner table conversation might save more lives than the classroom lecture. A teacher who pauses for five minutes may accomplish more than the teacher who finishes the syllabus on time. The child who feels heard today may never know a loneliness that is unbearable tomorrow.

And no article can explain what happened in Amaira’s heart in those last moments. No investigation can ever erase the grief of her parents. No punishment can bring her back the future she was to have. But her story can still make a difference. It can change the way teachers respond to the next scared child. What parents think of the next weird silence. The effects of repeated cruelty as seen by classmates. How schools measure success — not only by grades and trophies, but by how safe the emotional health of every child who passes through their gates is. Maybe that would be the legacy that no family should ever have to create.

Every morning parents leave their children at the school gates based on extraordinary trust. They rely on teachers to teach them. They expect schools to be safe places. They think that childhood will remain unspoiled until the last bell is rung. That trust is holy. When it is broken, an entire society has to stop and reflect. Nonetheless, parents must actively enquire about anti-bullying mechanisms and counselling structures during parent-teacher meetings to prevent such incidents.

The unfortunate child’s desk is empty. Her books are shut. Her laugh is old in recollection. But her story still holds a question that resonates much further than one classroom in Jaipur: if a child folds her hands in front of the teachers who are supposed to care for her, will someone stop, listen and protect her? How we answer that question will determine the future of our schools and the character of our society. Because education starts with literacy. But civilisation starts with kindness.

aufaq.zargar@gmail.com
